name: Italian

ancestors.notes: Italo-Romance Vulgar Latin: gemination preserved, 7-vowel system, -s lost, standard based on Tuscan.
Lombardic superstrate (6th–8th c.): vocabulary (guancia, stinco, schiena), some N. Italian phonological influence.
Ostrogothic superstrate (5th–6th c.): limited phonological impact, some vocabulary.
Greek substrate (Magna Graecia): mainly affects southern dialects; limited in Tuscan standard.

notes: Standard Italian (based on Florentine/Tuscan). Open/close mid-vowel distinction (e/ɛ, o/ɔ) is lexically determined and varies by region. Gemination is phonemic (fato/fatto). Gorgia toscana (intervocalic stop aspiration) is a regional Tuscan feature, not standard. C/G SOFTENING: c→[tʃ] and g→[dʒ] before e/i (ci, ce, gi, ge); [k]/[ɡ] elsewhere. INTERVOCALIC s: [z] between vowels in standard Italian (N. Italy); [s] word-initially. Z: [dz] word-initially and post-consonantally, [ts] in other positions. SC: [ʃ] before e/i, [sk] elsewhere. GEMINATE SOFTENING: the doubled spellings ⟨cc⟩ and ⟨gg⟩ take whichever value the following vowel selects, so they are [ttʃ] and [ddʒ] before e/i and [kk]/[ɡɡ] elsewhere (leggo [leɡɡo] vs legge [leddʒe]); in the geminate affricate only the stop portion is long (Krämer 2009 §2.2, §7.1; Rogers & d'Arcangeli 2004). ⟨cci⟩/⟨ggi⟩ are the geminate counterparts of ⟨ci⟩/⟨gi⟩ and mute the ⟨i⟩ before a vowel (faccia [fattʃa], maggio [maddʒo]). PRECONSONANTAL s: no voicing contrast is available before a consonant — [z] before every voiced consonant (sbagliare, smettere, snello, slitta, sradicare, svelto, asma), [s] before every voiceless one (spero, stella, sfida) (Bertinetto & Loporcaro 2005; Krämer 2009 §5.3). GU: ⟨gu⟩ before a vowel spells /ɡw/, the voiced counterpart of ⟨qu⟩ (guerra, guida, seguire); before a consonant the ⟨u⟩ is an ordinary vowel (gustare) (Rogers & d'Arcangeli 2004; Krämer 2009 §2.2). CEILINGS (not expressible from the orthography, and left to a downstream lexicon), with the share of residual error each accounts for on the full it/wikipron gold: the open/close mid-vowel choice is lexical and etymological and unmarked in the spelling (58% of residual error); the [ts]/[dz] value of ⟨z⟩ and ⟨zz⟩ is lexical, azzurro [addzurro] against pizza [pittsa] (12%); glide-versus-hiatus for prevocalic ⟨i u⟩ turns on stress and syllabification, Adriana [adriana] against piano [pjano], and Italian stress is not orthographically recoverable beyond the accented subset (13%); the Tuscan/Northern split in intervocalic ⟨s⟩ is varietal, so one spec cannot satisfy both and this one states the Standard Northern [z] (9%). Preconsonantal ⟨s⟩ voicing, by contrast, is pan-Italian and holds in Florence and Rome as well, so the four parent:it-IT central varieties inherit it deliberately (Bertinetto & Loporcaro 2005; Canepari 2009). Raddoppiamento fonosintattico is cross-word and belongs to the sandhi layer. Sources: Lepschy & Lepschy (1988), Maiden (1995), Rogers & d'Arcangeli (2004), Bertinetto & Loporcaro (2005), Krämer (2009), Canepari (2009).

stress.notes: Italian stress: written accents (à è é ì ò ó ù) always mark the stressed syllable and override position rules. Without an accent mark the default is paroxytone (penultimate). Proparoxytones (tavola, àlbero, pàgina) are lexical and undetectable from orthography alone — a written accent is not compulsory on them in standard Italian; they cannot be reliably predicted by rule. This block therefore uses default -2 (paroxytone) and relies on marked_vowels to handle the accented subset. Unaccented antepenultimate stress is not predicted.

allophone_rules.notes: Intervocalic /ɲ/ is inherently long in Italian (Krämer (2009) The Phonology of Italian (OUP) §7.2; Canepari DiPI): bagno [baɲɲo], aglio [aʎʎo], pesce [peʃʃe], vizio [vittsjo].
Intervocalic /ʎ/ is inherently long in Italian (Krämer (2009) The Phonology of Italian (OUP) §7.2; Canepari DiPI): bagno [baɲɲo], aglio [aʎʎo], pesce [peʃʃe], vizio [vittsjo].
Intervocalic /ʃ/ is inherently long in Italian (Krämer (2009) The Phonology of Italian (OUP) §7.2; Canepari DiPI): bagno [baɲɲo], aglio [aʎʎo], pesce [peʃʃe], vizio [vittsjo].
Intervocalic /ts/ is inherently long in Italian (Krämer (2009) The Phonology of Italian (OUP) §7.2; Canepari DiPI): bagno [baɲɲo], aglio [aʎʎo], pesce [peʃʃe], vizio [vittsjo].
Intervocalic /dz/ is inherently long in Italian (Krämer (2009) The Phonology of Italian (OUP) §7.2; Canepari DiPI): bagno [baɲɲo], aglio [aʎʎo], pesce [peʃʃe], vizio [vittsjo].

Preconsonantal /s/ agrees in voicing with the following consonant: [z] before any voiced consonant, [s] before any voiceless one, with no contrast available in that position (Bertinetto & Loporcaro (2005) JIPA 35(2) 131-151, 'Consonants'; Krämer (2009) The Phonology of Italian (OUP) §5.3). sbagliare [zbaʎʎare], smettere [zmettere], snello [znɛllo], slitta [zlitta], sradicare [zradikare], svelto [zvɛlto], asma [azma] — against spero [spɛro], stella [stella], sfida [sfida].
